performers: John Harrison, violin; Wichita State University Chamber Players; Robert Turizziani, conductor
intro: The finale of Spring, RV 269, from Vivaldi’s The Four Seasons is a Danza pastorale for nymphs and shepherds, in which the violins play over the long E and B of a country bagpipe. The dance moves into C♯ minor and E minor before it returns to the home key.

sections.label: A · The bagpipe dance
sections.mNote: A violin tune above long-held E and B

sections.label: B · The soloist leaves the drone
sections.mNote: Rising sequences and a chromatic bass lead towards C♯ minor

sections.label: A′ · Refrain in C♯ minor
sections.mNote: The refrain returns in C♯ minor and moves to B major.

sections.label: C · Solo violin episode with strings
sections.mNote: The solo moves through several keys over sustained bass notes.

sections.label: A″ · Dance refrain in E minor
sections.mNote: The refrain begins in E major, then G♯ becomes G♮.

sections.label: D · Solo violin over pedal B
sections.mNote: The bass holds B while the upper strings rest.

sections.label: A · The last E-major dance
sections.mNote: The full strings return to E major

cues.title: Bagpipe drone in the bass
cues.text: “Di pastoral Zampogna al Suon festante” — “To the merry sound of a shepherd’s bagpipe.” The 1725 sonnet names the instrument for this dance. Long E and B notes in the bass imitate the bagpipe’s drone, and the violin tune moves in four groups of three quavers.
cues.evidence: Spring sonnet, letter G; translation ours. Mutopia score after Performers’ Facsimiles, III, bars 1–12, marked Danza Pastorale in 12/8: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The dance in C♯ minor
cues.text: The strings play the rocking dance again, now in C♯ minor. The bass holds C♯ where it first held E. It then moves again, and the tune passes through E major towards B major.
cues.evidence: Mutopia score, III, bars 22–34; José Rodríguez Alvira traces the progression: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/03.php.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Spring sonnet, final lines, 1725
cues.text: “Danzan Ninfe e Pastor nel tetto amato / Di primavera all’apparir brillante” — “Nymphs and shepherds dance beneath their beloved shelter at spring’s brilliant arrival.” The sonnet places mythological nymphs beside working shepherds, and both dance to the same country dance.
cues.evidence: Spring sonnet, 1725, final two lines, letter G; translation ours. The text is printed with the Mutopia score and reproduced at https://nac-cna.ca/en/event/notes/36996. The sonnets were published anonymously.

cues.title: First opera, Vicenza, 1713
cues.text: In May 1713 Vivaldi’s first opera entirely his own, Ottone in villa, was given in Vicenza, away from the censorious eyes of his fellow Venetians. It was a success. He followed it with the oratorio La vittoria navale and then returned to Venice.
cues.evidence: Michael Talbot, Vivaldi, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani: 1713 as the year of his first opera and oratorio entirely from his own pen; Ottone in villa (libretto by Domenico Lalli) given in May at Vicenza, a stage outside Venice chosen to shield his debut from his fellow citizens’ censorious eyes; its success; then the oratorio La vittoria navale before his return to Venice. https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/antonio-vivaldi_%28Dizionario-Biografico%29/

cues.title: Turn to E minor
cues.text: The dance returns in E major, then turns to E minor. G♯ becomes G♮, and the bass descends by semitones beneath the dance rhythm.
cues.evidence: Mutopia score, III, bars 58–70, including the change to E minor in bar 61 and chromatic bass descent; commentary at https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/03.php.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First edition, Amsterdam, 1725
cues.text: The Amsterdam publisher Le Cène issued the Seasons in 1725 as the first four of the twelve concertos in Op. 8, Il cimento dell’armonia e dell’inventione. They were dedicated to Count Wenzel von Morzin, who had known them for some years. No autograph survives.
cues.evidence: Michael Talbot, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani (Op. VIII published by Le Cène, Amsterdam, 1725, dedicated to Count Wenzel von Morzin, whom Vivaldi had served for several years); IMSLP’s record of the first edition. Paul Everett, Vivaldi: The Four Seasons and Other Concertos, Op. 8 (Cambridge Music Handbooks, 1996), on the dedication letter: the Seasons were music Morzin already possessed. Martin Pearlman’s Boston Baroque note: no surviving autograph. https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/antonio-vivaldi_%28Dizionario-Biografico%29/ https://imslp.org/wiki/Il_cimento_dell'armonia_e_dell'inventione,_Op.8_(Vivaldi,_Antonio) https://baroque.boston/vivaldi-four-seasons

cues.title: Return to E major
cues.text: The long bass B resolves to E, and the full strings return to the dance in the major key (bars 79–89). The final phrase is repeated piano as an echo.
cues.evidence: Mutopia score, III, bars 79–89, with the return to E major and the later piano echo: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The bass leaves the E pedal
transitions.to: B · The soloist leaves the drone
transitions.how: The solo violin leaves the full-string dance while the bass holds E. The bass then begins to move, and ascending sequences pass through A and B towards C♯ minor. A descent by semitones leads into the next refrain.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, III, bars 12–22; bass and harmonic route shown at https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/03.php.

transitions.title: Return to the dance in C♯ minor
transitions.from: B · The soloist leaves the drone
transitions.how: The bass resolves G♯ to C♯. The full strings resume the opening dance in C♯ minor over a long C♯ pedal. The dotted rhythm is kept unchanged. A descending-fifths progression then takes the phrase through E major towards B major.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, III, bars 21–34; harmonic sequence explained at https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/03.php.

transitions.title: Cadence in B major and solo episode
transitions.to: C · Solo violin episode with strings
transitions.how: The bass moves E–F♯–B at the cadence. The soloist begins a new episode in B major, with short bass notes punctuating the phrase. A chain of fifths moves through E, A and D, and the harmony then returns to B.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, III, bars 33–58; key sequence in Rodríguez Alvira’s commentary: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/03.php.

transitions.title: The dance refrain turns to E minor
transitions.from: C · Solo violin episode with strings
transitions.to: A″ · Dance refrain in E minor
transitions.how: The solo episode ends in B major. The bass returns to its long E and the strings begin the dance in E major. At bar 61 the key signature changes to one sharp. G♮ replaces G♯, and the refrain continues in E minor.

transitions.title: A long B under the solo
transitions.from: A″ · Dance refrain in E minor
transitions.to: D · Solo violin over pedal B
transitions.how: The bass descends E–D♯–D–C♯–C–B and holds the B. The orchestral violins stop, and the soloist plays above this dominant pedal. The B is held through the episode until the final return to E major.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, III, bars 68–79, bass descent and sustained B: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301.

transitions.title: E major after the long B
transitions.from: D · Solo violin over pedal B
transitions.how: The bass moves from its long B to E, and the full strings resume the dance in E major. The soloist rejoins the orchestral violins. Long E and B notes support the last phrases, including their piano echo.

source.title: Vivaldi, The Four Seasons — Mutopia score after Performers’ Facsimiles
source.locator: III. Allegro, especially bars 1–14, 22, 34–58, 71–89. Passage-level participation, not individual attack alignment; cellos/basses represent the written basso part, with no claim about keyboard realization.

timeline.note: Full-string dance over sustained bass notes.
First solo episode; the orchestral upper strings rest while the basso accompanies the violin.
The minor-key refrain brings back the full strings.
Extended solo-led passage; upper strings answer and the bass later rests, so this is passage-level participation.
The refrain returns and changes from E major to E minor.
Solo violin over the sustained B bass; orchestral violins rest.
The closing dance, for full strings, returns to E major.

composer.epithet: Venetian composer of concertos for the women of the Pietà and operas for the city’s theatres, who wrote a barking dog for the viola.
facts: Violin with his father Giovanni Battista, a player at St Mark’s, Venice
Pietà violin teacher from 1703; maestro de’ concerti from 1716; court service in Mantua, 1718–20
More than 500 concertos, operas, sacred music and sonatas
composer.background:
In 1703 Antonio Vivaldi, a twenty-five-year-old Venetian, was ordained priest in March and became a violin teacher in September. He had red hair, a formidable bow arm and a chest complaint that made celebrating Mass difficult. His father Giovanni Battista had been a barber before joining the violinists at St Mark’s; he taught Antonio and went on helping with his career long after the son had become famous. In Venice Antonio was known as il prete rosso, the red priest. He worked in the chapel, the orchestra gallery and the opera house.

The Ospedale della Pietà cared for abandoned children. Its musical establishment was a selected group of girls and women, trained to sing and play to a standard that brought visitors from across Europe. Some remained there as adult musicians and teachers. Vivaldi taught the advanced string players, rehearsed the orchestra and supplied new pieces. The governors voted on his employment each year. In 1709 they dispensed with him, and in 1711 they took him back.
